After living in the Howard Beach area for over 10 years, I finally got a chance to try Bruno’s. Based on many of the reviews I’d seen beforehand, the lower-rated ones turned out to be pretty accurate.

Let’s start with the service, it was good. Several waiters stopped by to check if we were ready to order, and they brought out bread for the table to snack on. One waiter also presented a tray of meats and seafood specials for the night, which felt like a classic touch you don’t see much anymore. I appreciated that tradition. We went on a random weeknight after work and had no trouble getting seated.

For starters, we ordered the calamari arrabbiata and a margherita pizza. Both were solid, the pizza, in particular, was spot on, clearly made fresh in their pizza oven.

The main courses took a bit longer to arrive, and unfortunately, they were all slightly underseasoned. I had the tomahawk pork chop, which was nicely grilled but could have used more salt. One friend ordered the veal marsala, which had the same issue, and another got the scallops, good size and portion, but again, just a bit underseasoned.

Overall, it’s a nice local spot worth checking out. If you’re in the mood for Italian and haven’t tried Bruno’s yet, it’s still worth a visit, especially to support a neighborhood restaurant.

text.text:
TL;DR: Halal Burmese joint with excellent curries in particular. Might be closer to a 4, but I'll bump it up until I try it again

I went to the new Burmese Bites location with a group about a week ago, having had their food before at the Queens Night Market but never having unfortunately gone to their whole location in a mall in Elmhurst. There were many people waiting for tables or takeout while we were eating, and especially afterward, so you may want to come early.

The first dish that arrived was their alright take on the Burmese national dish, Mohinga for $15. As we were splitting everything, they provided bowls and extra spoons for everyone, and the portion was definitely decent for the price. The dish was decent, but it felt like it was missing something. I like the amount of fritters, but I wish there were more banana blossom for texture. I also felt the flavor was a bit too light compared to either Sophie's or Asian Bowl, and less thick. I'm not sure if it's because they're straining it too much, but the dish needed the fish sauce on the table to add more flavor, which is usually not the case. The most comparable version is at Little Myanmar, which definitely isn't my favorite version of this soup.

The other comparable dish, but better, was the Lahpet Thoke for the same price. Compared to other places, the size was between Asian Bowl and Sophie's, and the flavor was much better than Asian Bowl's, as theirs was a bit wet. The dish otherwise had a nice fermented flavor with a good amount of crunchiness, as it should, though it could have used a little bit more heat. Overall, I liked it, with the only better version being the much more expensive one at Little Myanmar.

Our only other appetizer was something I added to the meal. This was their excellent Keema Palata for $12. I decided to add this partially because I love this dish, and it was one of the things I liked a lot when they served it at the Night Market. The portion was plentiful, and the chicken inside was well spiced with a bit of butteriness from the palata, which is the Burmese version of a paratha, of course. I guess the only complaint I can make is that some of the crust felt a bit overcooked, but not so much that it wasn't enjoyable. I would recommend this.

The other main dishes all came with rice and were less comparable and better. My favorite, barely, was the NgaShint Chaut Sat for $25. It reminded me of a better version of a similar dish you can find in many Szechuan spots. By comparison, the dish had a nice mix of sweetness and spice with a definite kick. I also preferred the eel, as it was cut up into bigger pieces and it wasn't overly fried, so you could still get a bit of texture. The fried garlic added a nice aroma throughout the dish, as well as some good crunch, along with the chili and other spices. This was wonderful.

Most people's favorite was the $19 Ah Meh Tha Hin. The beef itself was fork-tender, so a knife wasn't necessary. The spices from the rather thick curry included some nice herbal sourness from the lemongrass, along with some heat and a bit of sweetness. Due to the thickness and spices, the curry reminded me, to an extent, of some semi-dry rendangs, but less coconut-forward and a bit less fiery. I would highly recommend this.

The last dish was the other $19 curry, the Nga Hin. The fish in this case was swai, or basa/catfish. The fish itself was tender, but it didn't fully fall apart in the curry, which I liked, as it kept some texture. The curry itself was on the slightly sour end, but not too much for any of our palates. This was also very tasty, and I would recommend it if you want a curry that is flavorful but not spicy.

I would prefer to go back to this place before giving it a true rating to try the Shan Noodles and other dishes I am more familiar with, but based on what I tried, I liked it. This is another nice option in the area for those looking for a different halal food experience, and it's great if you're not in the mood to go to Elmhurst for other Burmese options.

Marani Grill is one of those places that feels steady the moment you walk in 🇬🇪

The food leans into traditional Georgian cooking in a way that doesn’t feel adjusted for anything else—just straightforward, home-style flavors. The khachapuri comes out warm and balanced 🫓, the grilled meats are well-seasoned without being heavy 🔥, and everything feels like it was made with familiarity rather than overthinking. It’s the kind of meal where the dishes don’t compete with each other; they just work together.

What stood out most is how consistent everything felt across the table—nothing overly complicated, just solid execution of classic dishes that you’d expect in a Georgian home or a family-run spot.

Overall, it’s a reliable spot if you want authentic Georgian food that keeps things simple and grounded rather than trying to reinvent anything 🍽️✨

Samosa was perfect. The Goat Mandras was my favorite with a sauce that has spice but not super spicy considering the red chili symbol. Chicken Tikka was also very good. My garlic naan was SO good, has a crunch on one side but airy soft to bite. Unlimited little rice bowls?! This will be our go-to Indian after our first experience.
